text: The increase in anthropogenically-induced stressors is intensifying the biodiversity crisis. These 50 threats impact species across the tree of life and globe. The field of conservation genomics can 51 inform conservation actions to curb the loss of biodiversity. However, without widespread use of 52 appropriate methods, few species will benefit. The annual “ConGen” training course provides 53 students, early-career scientists, and practitioners an opportunity to broaden their exposure and 54 gain practical skills in conservation genomics. Here, we review outcomes of ConGen 2021 by 55 highlighting practical guidance and considerations for applied conservation genomics and online 56 courses. We share insights aimed at ensuring the effectiveness of conservation actions around 57 three themes: (1) expanding training in computation and conservation genomics, (2) conducting 58 rigorous, theory-based population genomics, and (3) facilitating communication and 59 collaboration among stakeholders. We provide advice on topics such as choosing DNA marker 60 types, using improved pipelines with STACKS, sequencing and assembling genomes, detecting 61 selection, correcting for multiple testing, estimating real-time gene flow, designing hands-on 62 learning exercises, and bridging the conservation genetic gap. Additionally, we make available 63 some conservation genomics software, lecture videos, weblinks, and other training tools used in 64 ConGen 2021.This review aims to help students and professionals expand their conservation 65 toolkit to include genomic principles and approaches for managing and conserving biodiversity.

As the field expands and as genomic data become more easily generated, there is a growing 86 need to train students, early-career scientists, and practitioners in the application of relevant 87 tools to address diverse conservation issues (Schweizer et al., 2021; Taylor, Dussex, & van 89 To provide accessible conservation genomics training to a geographically broad group of 90 students and professionals, experts in the field convene annually to teach a 1–2 week-long 91 course, called “ConGen”, which focuses on population genetic analyses for conservation 92 applications, based at the University of Montana, USA 93 (https://www.umt.edu/ces/conferences/congen). In this review, we discuss three major themes 94 that emerged during the virtual ConGen 2021 course that have not already been covered in past 95 meeting reviews (e.g., K. R. Andrews & Luikart, 2014; Benestan et al., 2016; Hendricks et al., 96 2018; Schweizer et al., 2021; Stahlke et al., 2020).

First, expanding and enriching training in conservation genomics is needed to make the 98 population genomics toolkit more accessible to a global population of concerned scientists, 99 managers, and policymakers; we highlight training approaches that ConGen 2021 has taken 100 and we offer recommendations for future virtual workshops. Second, we continue to build on the 101 ConGen foundation that conducting rigorous science rooted in theory is necessary to generate 102 actionable information (Allendorf, 2017). This principle must be implemented throughout the 103 population genomics research pipeline — from considering the appropriate molecular marker(s) 104 for a research question, to avoiding pitfalls associated with data analysis, interpretation, and 105 practical applications. Third, we discuss how population genomic knowledge and tools are 106 ineffectual without the involvement of partners and practitioners equipped to put them into 107 action; here we emphasize how building collaborations that foster communication among 108 stakeholders is needed to promote better conservation outcomes (Taylor et al., 2017).

Considering this, 199 ConGen 2021 training focused specifically on integrating the principles or assumptions of 200 population genomics tests, alongside applications of tests and interpretations of results in 201 practical scenarios (e.g., Table 1). Dr. Norah Saarman led an exemplary module, in terms of 202 clear learning goals and attributes that facilitated learning; she walked ConGen 2021 203 participants through a series of activities exploring Hardy-Weinberg (HW) proportions and 205 Among the most important, yet often poorly executed and interpreted, tests in population 206 genetics are tests for HW proportions (Waples, 2014); the number of tests has increased with 207 high-throughput sequencing datasets (Graffelman & Weir, 2018; Sethuraman et al., 2019).

Learning goals from the ConGen 2021 module included deepening understanding of 209 assumptions and applications of the HW principle to detect signatures of various demographic 210 patterns (e.g., population structure, admixture) and identify the impact of study design and data 211 collection (e.g., sequencing depth, genotyping error) on the interpretation of tests for HW 212 proportions (see link to Norah Saarman’s hands-on exercise in Table 1). Secondary goals were 213 to estimate locus-by-locus FIS and mean FIS in R, and to distinguish between causes of HW 214 deviations including Wahlund effect (substructure) versus effects of small Ne and drift, and 216 ConGen participants used the HIERFSTAT package (Goudet, 2005) in R to explore how 217 population structure, admixture, finite populations, and data sources (e.g., natural population, 218 GWAS experiment) can impact interpretation of tests for HW proportions. In the first activity, 219 students calculated and plotted basic statistics, including FIS, for four simulated datasets — 220 small Ne, outlier loci, population substructure, and a healthy (random mating) population in HW 221 proportions. Participants did not know which scenario (e.g. small Ne, etc.) their simulated data 222 originated from. Participants then used the output plots to infer which scenario of the four 223 hypothetical scenarios their data originated from (Figure 1). In the second activity, students 224 simulated two datasets and estimated basic statistics using HIERFSTAT, then performed a PCA 225 using the ADEGENET package (Jombart, 2008) in R. The outputs were used to distinguish 226 signatures of population structure from signatures of strong inbreeding in an idealized (Wright- 228 This activity-based teaching module emphasized skill development and practice for 229 estimating HW proportions and interpreting statistical results using genetic datasets simulating 230 various deviations from HW proportions. By using simulations, students had the opportunity to 231 analyze datasets as if they were empirical studies, interpret results, and discuss putative drivers 232 of the recovered signal with the instructor and class, where the correct answer was known 233 (Figure 1). For example, one of the four simulated scenarios presented with an excess of 234 heterozygotes at most loci, but students did not know if the dataset deviated from HW 235 proportions. Students worked together in Zoom breakout rooms before discussing their findings 236 with the entire class, focusing on population parameters (in this case, negative FIS across loci), 237 as well as genome-wide and locus-specific patterns (such as differences in allele frequencies 238 between the sexes caused by drift and small Ne). The general discussion included considering 239 how to test for an excess of heterozygotes and allele frequency differences between sexes, 240 which can be done separately or simultaneously (e.g., Graffelman & Weir, 2018), and how to 241 estimate Ne to follow-up this hypothesis that Ne is small (e.g., Waples & Do, 2010). This hands- 242 on teaching strategy using simulated genomic data can be applied to teaching interpretation of 243 other statistical tests or population metrics. By using simulated data that mimic various 244 scenarios seen in empirical conservation datasets, students received multiple forms of highly 245 applicable instruction and suggestions for best practices for data analysis and interpretation.

The field of conservation biology increasingly requires data science skills that are different from 249 traditional biology. Bioinformatics, or the processing and analysis of biological data, itself 250 encompasses skill sets that may include 1) large-scale data analysis, 2) programming, and 3) 251 computational communication skills (e.g., generating informative figures). Expertise in any one 252 of these skill sets can lay the groundwork for different career options, yet as research scientists 253 analyzing biological data, proficiency with all three is needed. Because these skills are important 254 components of conservation genomics, ConGen provided pre-conference sessions (see Table 255 1), suggested topical readings, and provided real-time trouble-shooting during the workshop 256 from experienced coders to help participants develop and practice these skills.
Data science skills are those that enable interaction with and analysis of large data sets.

These skills include basic computational proficiencies, such as the ability to navigate file 259 systems in a text-based environment, conduct exploratory data analyses, and interact with 260 remote computers, such as with institutional clusters or cloud-based servers (e.g., see tutorials 261 in Table 1). One of the most important responsibilities for a conservation genomicist will be 262 running software developed by others. This means familiarizing oneself with the standards and 263 paradigms of software development, including file formats and command line options. Once 264 comfortable with these abilities, more advanced skills become valuable, including optimization 265 of workflows through parallel computing using high-performance computing (HPC) clusters, 266 along with job scheduling software like SLURM and workflow development and management 267 software like SNAKEMAKE (Mölder et al., 2021) or NEXTFLOW (https://www.nextflow.io/index.html), 269 An additional skill that is crucial for data science in conservation is the ability to conduct 270 statistical analyses using open-source programming languages such as R. Open-source 271 software is freely available, lending itself to wide usage. Additionally, many packages have been 272 written for R that enable field-specific analyses (e.g., Paradis, 2020). By becoming proficient in 273 these types of languages, conservation biologists can analyze large data sets in an efficient and 274 reproducible manner. An excellent resource for learning about these skills at any level is the 275 book ‘Bioinformatics Data Skills’ (Buffalo, 2015).

While some knowledge of scripting is necessary and can facilitate the above data 277 science skills, there may occasionally become a point when the best way to understand or 278 implement a method is to code it oneself, or one may even wish to develop and share their own 279 method through novel software. In this case, a different set of skills is needed. Programming 280 skills are closely entwined with data science skills, but also require an eye for algorithm 281 development and efficiency. While each programming language has its pros and cons, which 282 may make one language more appropriate for certain tasks than others, many programming 283 skills, like general problem solving, are applicable across languages. This means that a novice 284 might pick one language to master before translating that knowledge to a different language. By 285 mastering these general skills first, learning the way a new language is typed, or its syntax, 286 becomes an easier task. By far the most common programming languages for bioinformatics 287 are high-level scripting languages like Python (www.python.org) and R (www.r-project.org).

However, some software development is also done in C/C++ or Java, therefore, one of those 289 might be a favorable choice for a second language. To learn to program there is no better 290 method than to solve problems with code, and there are many tutorials and resources online to 291 facilitate this. For Python, we recommend Rosalind (https://rosalind.info), a bioinformatics 292 specific set of Python programming problems that start from the most basic (installing Python) to 293 very advanced (e.g., sequence alignment, genome assembly).

The final step in a project is to translate the patterns observed in large datasets into 295 more easily digestible concise forms like figures, papers, and talks. This is distinct from science 296 communication — a field on its own focused on conveying complex scientific ideas to the public, 297 for which there are many quality resources available to help non-professionals (e.g., Hochberg 298 & Hochberg, 2019). Rather, this set of computational communication skills is much the same as 299 for any scientist wishing to share their work with their peers, though at a larger, often genome- 300 wide scale. Skills that help facilitate this communication include data visualization with R and 301 possibly a vector graphics program like Adobe Illustrator, statistical analysis in R, word 302 processing with collaboration through cloud-based services, and even web design. Rigorous science at each step of the data analysis pipeline 310 This section discusses novel developments or timely issues associated with seven important 311 topics covered at ConGen 2021. Highlights include how to choose the best molecular marker(s) 312 for a given study system and research question (2.1), which is particularly important when 313 working with rare and endangered species and a limited budget or sample sizes; that we should 314 consider identifying structural variants (in addition to SNPs) because they are abundant across 315 genomes and often influence phenotypes and fitness (2.2); how to appropriately process 316 molecular genetic data, including filtering and analyzing RADseq data from raw reads to 317 genotypes using STACKS version v2 (2.3). We also discuss which factors to consider when 318 assembling reference genomes, such as genome size, ploidy, heterozygosity, sample quality 319 and quantity (2.4); how to detect selection signatures including the use of a flexible approach 320 not requiring parental population identification, as implemented in PCADAPT (2.5); and the 321 advantages and limitations of estimating dispersal rates using BAYESASS (2.6). Finally, we 322 illustrate the importance of correcting for multiple testing (2.7).

Recent advances in sequencing technology, and associated cost reductions, have shifted 326 applications towards reduced-representation sequencing, genotyping-by-sequencing (GBS), 327 and low-coverage whole-genome sequencing approaches (Ali et al., 2016; Baird et al., 2008;

Campbell, Harmon, & Narum, 2015; Lou, Jacobs, Wilder, & Therkildsen, 2021) — provide 329 researchers with tools to reach specific conservation goals. However, the wide variety of 330 available approaches can lead to uncertainty and confusion when selecting the most 331 appropriate marker type or sampling method. Indeed, while there is broad understanding that 332 specific study questions and the biology of target organisms must guide the selection of 333 molecular methods, many nuanced factors involved in these decisions remain (e.g., Hohenlohe, 334 Hand, Andrews, & Luikart, 2019; Meek & Larson, 2019).

In the current field of conservation genetics, studies often address a combination of 336 questions relating to variation at putatively neutral and adaptive regions of the genome. Such 337 studies have traditionally addressed questions relating to population structure, relative diversity, 338 pedigrees, relatedness, and phylogenetic relationships with a modest set of putatively neutral 339 markers (Hohenlohe et al., 2019; Schweizer et al., 2021). Research questions that aim to 340 address selective processes within or between species, populations, ecotypes, or phenotypes 341 typically require markers from adaptive regions of the genome. While there remain cases where 342 microsatellites are fully adequate, there are many scenarios where larger panels of genome- 343 wide markers may be less costly (Campbell et al., 2015) or allow investigation of both neutral 344 and adaptive variation (e.g., Lou et al., 2021; Meek & Larson, 2019).

Based on these concepts, the flow chart in Figure 2 is intended to help researchers 346 select an appropriate marker method for their study question. The chart begins with the 347 question: “Does the study question require both neutral and adaptive markers?”, to lead 348 researchers along various paths to reach methods that would be applicable in most 349 circumstances. This chart is not intended to be comprehensive of all scenarios, and largely 350 covers sequencing or GBS-based endpoints for conservation genomics. Other tools are 351 recommended for specialized applications (reviewed in Hohenlohe et al., 2019; Schweizer et al., 352 2021), such as epigenetics and gene expression (Anastasiadi, Venney, Bernatchez, & 353 Wellenreuther, 2021), genome assembly (Whibley, Kelley, & Narum, 2021), or environmental 354 DNA (Rodríguez-Ezpeleta et al., 2021). Furthermore, decisions regarding the discovery of 355 markers throughout the genome will typically involve factors of both scientific (e.g., sample size, 356 genome size, statistical power, evolutionary context) and practical natures (e.g., sample quality, 357 funding, time, resources, career goals). Conducting quality control in RADseq analysis 363 Among the most important breakthroughs in the 2010s for conservation genetics was the 364 development of Restriction site-Associated DNA sequencing (RADseq; Anonymous, 2010). This 365 sequencing approach has become indispensable in modern conservation genomics due to its 366 applicability across many biological systems and research questions, particularly in those 367 lacking a reference genome (Bootsma, Miller, Sass, Euclide, & Larson, 2021; Garrison, 368 Johnson, & Whelan, 2021; Nash et al., 2018; Stuart et al., 2014). However, successful 369 implementation of this method requires the proper management of key technical aspects, such 370 as marker density, sequencing coverage, and PCR duplicates to ensure that the true biological 371 signal is recovered (reviewed in K. R. Andrews, Good, Miller, Luikart, & Hohenlohe, 2016;

Factors such as low sequencing coverage and an excess of PCR duplicate 373 reads can negatively impact the accuracy of the inferred genotypes by leading to missing alleles 374 (allele dropout), which distorts the underlying information obtained from the library by, for 375 example, causing heterozygotes to be scored as homozygotes. Moreover, these technical 376 sources of error appear to be the primary source of allele dropout in RADseq experiments, far 377 eclipsing the effects of dropout caused by biological polymorphism (Rivera-Colón, Rochette, & 379 There are several analytical pipelines available for the analysis of RADseq data, 380 including STACKS 2 (Rochette, Rivera-Colón, & Catchen, 2019), DDOCENT (Puritz, Hollenbeck, & 381 Gold, 2014), IPYRAD (Eaton & Overcast, 2020), among others. While the underlying algorithmic 382 approaches might be different in each software, their results can all be negatively impacted by 383 these technical artifacts (e.g., low coverage and high duplicates). Therefore, monitoring the data 384 at each step of the pipeline should be an integral part of any RADseq analysis, regardless of the 385 software used. Although problems with coverage and duplicates originate from the construction 386 and sequencing of the library itself, steps can be taken post-sequencing to assess, and 387 potentially mitigate, their effects. For example, monitoring the distribution of reads across 388 samples when demultiplexing, verifying coverage before and after duplicate removal, and 389 filtering the resulting genotypes (see Box 1). These checks provide a robust and reliable 390 implementation of the library protocol, enabling the experimenter to trace the data (and problem 391 solve) at each major step of the analysis — from raw read to final genotype.

Comprehensive RADseq analysis using STACKS V2 394 The STACKS V2 software (Rochette et al., 2019) — a commonly used pipeline for assembling 395 and genotyping RADseq data — allows for easy monitoring of coverage and missing data at 396 different stages of the analysis (Cerca et al., 2021; Rivera-Colón & Catchen, 2021; Rochette & 397 Catchen, 2017). Using the stacks-dist-extract tool, distributed with the software, the user 398 can extract several tabular outputs containing detailed per-sample statistics from different logs 399 across the analysis. Below, we highlight examples of how this tool can be implemented to 400 assess the analysis at four stages of the pipeline: 1) during the processing of raw reads, 2) 401 when building de novo loci across samples, 3) in the finished, but unfiltered, catalog, and 4) in 402 the filtered loci and genotypes. See Rivera-Colón and Catchen (2021) for detailed examples.

After running process_radtags, which demultiplexes and cleans the raw reads, 404 stacks-dist-extract can be used to obtain a detailed per-sample breakdown of the 405 number of reads discarded and retained. This result is the earliest assessment of the 406 quality of the library. For example, an overall low number of retained reads will result in 407 downstream coverage problems across the analysis.

When running the de novo STACKS pipeline, the ustacks program builds loci in each 409 sample individually. At this stage, we see the first explicit measures of coverage at each 410 locus. Any patterns of low coverage at this stage will likely be further exacerbated in 411 downstream analyses. In addition to coverage, an important output to check is the 412 percentage of reads incorporated in the analysis. A high disparity in the number of reads 413 available and the number of reads retained across individuals can indicate problems with 414 the quality of individual samples, such as DNA contamination.

The finalized catalog for all RAD loci and genotypes is generated by the gstacks 416 software in both de novo and reference-based STACKS pipelines. Using stacks-dist- 417 extract to assess outputs at this stage of the analysis is critical, as we can obtain 418 information on the final depth of coverage, the number of called genotypes, and the 419 phasing of loci across individuals. A low proportion of phased loci might be indicative of 420 the presence of paralogs in the final loci preventing the generation of two haplotypes per 421 locus. When selected in the options, gstacks can also be used to remove PCR 422 duplicate reads from the final construction of the catalog. When this is performed, the 423 resulting coverage shown by the software will only include non-redundant reads and will 424 thus often be lower than the coverage shown by ustacks. Structural variants are major architects of genomic variation 438 Recent work has revealed that structural variants — variation that affects the presence, 439 abundance, position, and/or direction of a nucleotide sequence — are ubiquitous in nature, 440 often influence fitness, and can occupy larger sections of the genome relative to the more 441 commonly studied SNP variants (Catanach et al., 2019;

Structural variants are classified according to how they change a genome’s nucleotide 443 sequence. “Balanced” variants lead to a change in position or order, while “unbalanced” variants 444 involve the gain or loss of a nucleotide sequence (Mérot, Oomen, Tigano, & Wellenreuther, 445 2020). Balanced variants include inversions, fusions, fissions, translocations and larger changes 446 to sets of whole chromosomes (e.g., polyploidy), while unbalanced variants include small 447 insertions and deletions (indels) and copy number variants (CNVs), such as duplications. Both 448 balanced and unbalanced changes can affect the order and proximity of genetic elements and 449 this can consequently disrupt the functionality of extant genes, as well as lead to the creation of 450 new ones. All of these changes can also impact the three-dimensional structure of the genome, 451 which may influence gene expression and regulation (Mérot et al., 2020).

The role of structural variants in conservation and complementing SNP-based 453 approaches to enhance species recovery is increasingly realized (Wold et al., 2021). These 454 variants often detect significant genetic–environment associations where SNPs do not (e.g., sea 455 surface temperature and American lobsters, Homarus americanus

Structural information about the genome can also inform the management of different species, 457 and if these differences are fixed and thus diagnostic, simple molecular PCR tests can be 458 developed to inform management decisions (e.g., distinguishing a rare subspecies of white- 459 cheeked gibbon, Namascus leucogenys leucongenys As structural 460 variants can also reduce reproductive success, they are of interest to programs conserving 461 depleted species with small population sizes, and reproductive breakdowns (Deakin et al., 462 2019). A comprehensive characterization of the full spectrum of variation holds promise to 463 identify the causative mechanisms by which structural variants impact population dynamics, 464 reproductive success, and eco-evolutionary dynamics of endangered species.

The presence of structural variants can lead to genomic incompatibilities between 466 ancestral and novel variants that may influence hybridization and introgression, and can impact 467 the recombination landscape of the genome. Inversions are the most well studied structural 468 variants (reviewed in Wellenreuther & Bernatchez, 2018). They can lead to the formation of 469 secondary structures during meiosis in heterozygotes, thereby preventing the formation of 470 viable gametes (Sturtevant, 1913; Sturtevant & Mather, 1938). Likewise, fissions and fusions 471 can change the number and size of chromosomes, thereby impacting recombination rates even 473 As structural variants often occur in segments of genomes up to several Mb, they are 474 more likely to overlap gene and regulatory regions and reduce fitness. The impact on the 475 recombination landscape and the co-inheritance of potentially large haploblocks (i.e., linkage 476 disequilibrium-based genome blocks) means that structural variants can create large 477 supergenes (Charlesworth, 2016) and, indeed, several inversions are now referred to as 478 supergenes (Campagna, 2016). Moreover, the diverse impacts of structural variants means that 479 they commonly have a significant influence on the phenotype (Sanchis-Juan et al., 2018), as 480 seen in morphotypes of rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss: anadromous and resident 481 [Pearse, 2016)]) and the ruff bird (Calidris pugnax: satellites, faeders and independents 482

Structural variants are best assessed with high coverage whole-genome data (e.g., 484 NovaSeq), and long variants specifically should be targeted with long-read data (e.g., Pacific 485 Bioscience [PacBio]) that can span variant boundaries (Mahmoud et al., 2019). Other types of 486 sequencing data can also be used, e.g., paired-end data from reduced representation libraries 487 or data derived from standard shotgun libraries (i.e., with short insert size, generally <1 kb), but 488 their suitability in detecting a diverse set and size range of structural variants is more limited.

Detection of structural variants occurs via the application of both indirect and direct 490 methods. Indirect approaches apply unsupervised methods such as principal component 491 analysis (PCA) combined with information about linkage disequilibrium (LD) to detect genome 492 regions that co-segregate and show limited recombination, i.e., haploblocks (e.g., Mérot et al., 493 2021). Direct methods use information based on the read depth or from split reads and read 494 orientation to identify variants (e.g., duplications or deletions). Advancements, such as optical 495 mapping, Hi-C data and linked reads using 10xGenomics, all provide information to directly 496 detect structural variants de novo (Mérot et al., 2020). Software for the analysis of structural 497 variants is rapidly developing and continuously updated, and should be selected based on the 498 type of available data and structural variants of interest (e.g., LUMPY

Most work to date has focused on the adaptive significance of gene duplications and 501 large-effect inversions, with much less attention on other structural variant types, e.g., fusions or 502 translocations (Wellenreuther, Mérot, Berdan, & Bernatchez, 2019). Future studies should focus 503 on reproducible and well-documented frameworks for structural variant detection to uncover the 504 full spectrum of types and sizes of structural variants. Applying a general framework that is 505 based on solid structural variant discovery and includes empirical approaches to relate their 506 presence to their function and evolutionary significance (e.g., as outlined in Mérot et al., [2020]), 507 will facilitate comparative approaches and meta analyses that have not been possible to date. Applications and being an effective conservation genomicist 786 Conservation genomics is an applied science built on rigorous population genetics theory. The 787 main goal of conservation genetics is to provide information to improve the conservation and 788 management of biodiversity — from genes to species and ecosystems. Genomics has improved 789 many applications including assessing population structure, planning and monitoring 790 translocations and restoration, understanding gene flow and population connectivity through 791 landscape genomics analyses, invasive species management, identifying clonality and hybridity, 792 determining mating systems to understand population dynamics, and understanding 794 The most exciting power of genomics in conservation is the ability to investigate 795 knowledge gaps that couldn’t be addressed with previous types of molecular markers, such as 796 adaptation to climate change, which is critical for responding to changing conditions, and 797 understanding effects of inbreeding depression and the dynamics of small populations using 798 many neutral and adaptive loci (Allendorf et al. 2010). Genomics has been particularly powerful 799 in providing the means of assessing variation in adaptive regions of the genome, which is 800 important for facilitating adaptive responses of species to changing climates.

Adaptive variation has been investigated in many tree species, as this understanding 802 guides implementation of assisted gene flow (Aitken and Whitlock, (2013) and climate-assisted 803 provenancing (Prober et al., (2015) as a means of facilitating adaptation to changing climates.

Genomic analysis was used to understand adaptive variation in Corymbia calophylla, a key 805 species of the forests of south-western Australia. Association of SNP variants with precipitation 806 and temperature climatic variables, and mapping to Corymbia and Eucalyptus reference 807 genomes were used to identify the location and putative function of climate-associated variants 808 (Ahrens, Byrne, & Rymer, 2019). This genomic information is being combined with common 809 garden experiments (Ahrens et al., 2020) and ecophysiological analysis (Ahrens, Challis, et al., 810 2021) to provide an understanding of the species’ likely response to changing climate, and 811 inform adaptation strategies for forest conservation.

Landscape genomics allows association of variations in the genome with environmental 813 variables (also known as genotype-environment association studies), enabling inferences about 814 local adaptation (Rellstab, Gugerli, Eckert, Hancock, & Holderegger, 2015). For example, 815 genome-wide SNP frequencies of coral in New Caledonia were associated with remote-sensed 816 environmental heat data to investigate the local adaptation of reefs to thermal stress, where 817 candidate SNPs under selection were used to characterize the functional role of nearby genes 818 and make inferences about adaptive traits that could allow coral to persist in the face of 819 warming oceans (Selmoni et al., 2021). Similarly, RADseq data for the greenlip abalone 820 (Haliotis laevigata) revealed signs of local adaptation in candidate SNPs associated with genes 821 involved in tolerance to high temperature and low oxygen (Lampert, 2018; Sandoval-Castillo, 822 Robinson, Hart, Strain, & Beheregaray, 2018), with important implications for managing this 823 commercially important species in the face of climate change (Lopez, Kamel, Medina, Collins, & 825 Invasive species have major impacts on natural ecosystems (Scalera, Genovesi, Essl, & 826 Rabitsch, 2012) and this is likely to be exacerbated under climate change. Identification of the 827 origins of invasive species and their genetic diversity can be important for the design of control 828 strategies (particularly biological control methods), managing pathways of introduction, and 829 identifying adaptation in the introduced range. Genomics has been used to identify the origins of 830 Passiflora foetida, a climbing vine that is native to Central and South America, but has spread to 831 South-east Asia and the Pacific. In Australia, it has become a highly invasive weed that is 832 transforming ecosystems in the northern regions of the continent (Yockteng, d’Eeckenbrugge, & 833 Souza-Chies, 2011). Genome skimming was used to produce whole chloroplast and ITS 834 sequences from samples collected across the invasive range, that enabled efficient use of a 835 collection of herbarium specimens from across the native range held at Missouri Botanic 836 Gardens. The analysis showed evidence of three independent origins of the species into 837 Australia from Ecuador and Peru, Brazil, and the Caribbean, with only one of these lineages 838 becoming widespread (Hopley, Webber, Raghu, Morin, & Byrne, 2021). This has guided the 839 search for a biological control agent for this species.

While microsatellites have assisted the identification of species 842 boundaries, genomics has provided greater power to clarify entities in morphologically complex 843 groups. Furthermore, the analysis identified extensive clonality that 851 enabled the persistence and expansion of hybrids despite low fertility in F1s. This information 852 has enabled taxonomic revision of this group and clarification of species distributions to guide 853 management decisions in the geographic area. How to be an effective conservation geneticist 882 An effective conservation geneticist is first and foremost a capable population geneticist, with a 883 sound understanding of population genetic theory. This foundation is critical to effectively use 884 genomic data to aid conservation, particularly in the genomics era with a shift from few 885 molecular markers to many thousands or millions. Those aspiring to conduct conservation 886 genetics research should take courses on population genetics and gain experience by working 887 with a laboratory or organization with expertise in this area. In addition to acquiring the technical 888 acumen, developing skills that foster communication of genomics research and collaboration will 889 help the benefits of genetics to conservation become realized.
Genetic considerations can play important roles in effective conservation management, 891 but are often missing from conservation management planning and policy (Cook & Sgrò, 2017;

If this gap between population genomics research and 893 application persists, the tools and techniques described in previous sections will have limited 894 influence in practice. Thus, effective conservation geneticists need to understand the factors 895 that contribute to this gap and identify the tools and techniques we can use to bridge it.

Many factors may contribute to the lack of integration of genetic data into conservation 897 action plans. Hypotheses on drivers of the conservation genetics gap range from a lack of 898 awareness of the benefits of integrating genetics into conservation (Pierson et al., 2016), to 899 confusion stemming from heavy use of jargon in published communications (Hoban et al., 900 2013). Additionally, the perception that genetic consequences are a long-term problem resulting 901 from more immediate threats, may lead practitioners to prioritize shorter term problems such as 902 invasive predators (Jamieson, Wallis, & Briskie, 2006). Funding is also a consideration, where 903 practitioners may lack access to pay-to-view peer-reviewed publications (Cook & Sgrò, 2017), 904 genetics may be perceived as costly to implement (Vernesi & Bruford, 2009), or there may be a 905 lack of funding or other incentives to motivate geneticists to bridge the gap (Haig et al., 2016;

When conservation practitioners are asked specifically about why genetic data may 908 often be missing from conservation planning and management, a slightly different picture 909 emerges. Practitioners may struggle to close the gap due to a sense of insufficient knowledge of 910 genetics and are unsure of who to approach for help (Taylor et al., 2017). Practitioners typically 911 have a good understanding of how to manage genetic diversity in practical scenarios, but are 912 unfamiliar with the jargon inherent in the field (Cook & Sgrò, 2019). Moreover, practitioners are 913 not aware of the diverse scenarios where genetics can assist in conservation (Holderegger et 914 al., 2019; Taylor et al., 2017), and they don’t always understand the funding issues faced by 915 academic scientists (Taylor et al., 2017). Far from not understanding the benefits, practitioners 916 are usually very positive on the role of genetics in conservation and want to see genetic data 917 better integrated into management (Cook & Sgrò, 2018; Taft et al., 2020; Taylor et al., 2017).

The shift to genome-scale data could exacerbate the gap between population genomics 919 and its application in conservation. With the myriad benefits brought by genomics comes 920 additional jargon, workflow bottlenecks from the generation of massive amounts of data, and, in 921 some cases, increased costs. Some practitioners are concerned about the increased handling 922 time of vulnerable species needed to collect the high quality samples required for some 923 genomic work, while others are confused about the differences between genetics, genomics, 924 and genetically modified organisms (Kadykalo, Cooke, & Young, 2020). Genomics also has the 925 potential to further broaden the gap as the questions that practitioners need answered may be 926 misaligned with what researchers can publish in high impact journals. However, it is possible to 927 achieve both aims through effective communication and well-targeted research (see examples 929 Given the benefits of incorporating genetic data into conservation management, 930 geneticists and practitioners alike are keen to close the gap between knowledge and 931 application. Several strategies have been implemented to achieve this goal. In the USA, a 932 common approach is to have in-house geneticists embedded in agencies conducting 933 conservation activities such as the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), 934 Forest Service, and U.S. Geological Survey (USGS). Interestingly, practitioners surveyed in 935 New Zealand do not favor this model due to fears that resources could become monopolized by 936 certain teams. Instead, they prefer a model where collaborations are formed externally (Taylor 937 et al., 2017). An alternative strategy is to form boundary organizations — typically a collection of 938 researchers and practitioners from different organizations working together to bridge the gap via 939 communication and training (Cook, Mascia, Schwartz, Possingham, & Fuller, 2013).

Additionally, zoos can act as a useful bridge between conservation genetic research and 941 conservation practice. Eight zoos around the world have in-house genetics labs and well- 942 established functional partnerships with practitioners: the Antwerp Zoo, Chicago Zoological 943 Society, Copenhagen Zoo, Omaha’s Henry Doorly Zoo, Royal Zoological Society of Scotland, 944 San Diego Zoo Global, Smithsonian’s National Zoo, and South African National Biodiversity 946 Incorporating genetic metrics into the International Union for Conservation of Nature 947 (IUCN) RedList of threatened species would also be an effective motivator to gather and 948 analyze more genetic data for threatened species. Although integrating genetic data into threat 949 status can be challenging, it is not insurmountable (Funk, Forester, Converse, Darst, & Morey, 950 2019). Publishing in languages other than English (Holderegger et al., 2019) and producing 951 different versions of textbooks that cater to the needs of geneticists and practitioners (e.g., 952 Frankham et al., 2019) are also practical solutions for broadening access to and adoption of 953 conservation genomics approaches. Providing training for practitioners is another strategy to 954 address the gap, but one that requires investment of time from and development of training 956 Closing the conservation genetics gap is not a trivial effort and requires substantial 957 investments. As mentioned above, a good conservation geneticist is, first and foremost, a good 958 population geneticist. An effective conservation geneticist — one whose work is incorporated 959 into management and has positive implications for conservation — requires additional skills that 960 are often underappreciated in academic science programs.

After completing academic training in population genetics, a conservation geneticist can 962 follow numerous career paths, each requiring different skills. Those interested in big data 963 science must develop their bioinformatic skills (see section 1.3), while the more lab-orientated 964 might focus on experiments and genetic chemistry. Careers in conservation management might 965 require field experience and logistics management, and those forging a path in policy work will 966 need to understand political and legal processes and current affairs. These career directions 967 seem divergent, yet they all have one thing in common: they do not function independently.

Effective species conservation requires that conservation geneticists work together, in 969 partnership with other conservation practitioners, and that requires finely honed skills in 970 communication and collaboration. A conservation geneticist who can form collaborations with 971 those possessing complementary skills or knowledge, and who can communicate clearly about 972 their particular area of conservation genetics to broad audiences will be a far more effective 974 Soft skills like communication, and building and facilitating collaborations are under- 975 taught in academic science programs. Emergent conservation geneticists will likely have to seek 976 out experiences and additional training programs to sharpen the skills that will make them better 977 communicators and collaborators. Identifying advisors and colleagues who sit on threatened 978 species management steering groups and asking to sit in on meetings can be a rich learning 979 experience of the practicalities of working in such groups. Courses, such as the facilitation 980 training offered by the IUCN Conservation Planning Specialist Group (http://www.cpsg.org/our- 981 approach/training) or the structured decision-making training from the IUCN Conservation 982 Translocation Specialist Group (https://iucn-ctsg.org/), can help researchers practice using soft 983 skills to engage with conservation managers. Effort is required up front to obtain and hone these 984 skills, but the investment will reap benefits, making early career conservation geneticists more 985 employable in a competitive job market and, more importantly, making them more effective 989 The accelerating loss of biodiversity spurred by climate change, habitat loss, and other 990 stressors (Pörtner et al., 2021) elevates the need for rapid integration of population genomic 991 insights in conservation action plans (Allendorf et al., 2022; Hohenlohe et al., 2021; Kardos, 992 2021). The ConGen course serves as a conduit that delivers training needed to confront this 993 challenge. The COVID pandemic restricted our ability to offer an in-person course but created 994 the opportunity to reach an even broader audience by adapting the course to be offered 995 remotely (Section 1). This review highlights key emerging topics in conservation genomics 996 research, including the importance of understanding population genetics theory to ensure 997 appropriate data collection and analysis to address conservation concerns (Section 2) and 998 cultivating relationships with on-the-ground practitioners through effective communication 999 (Section 3). All loci that went to fixation during the simulations (e.g., panels A and C) are not shown because 1579 FIS cannot be estimated when there is zero heterozygosity.
